title: AI Town Hall — Halton Hills

panel.title: AI Town Hall
panel.assessment_scope: One assessment of the original replies; no further candidate questions or review rounds.

scores.strongest_point: An explicit pilot-and-measure approach connects investment decisions to oversight and resident access.
scores.biggest_gap: How municipal revenues, service demand and costs would change under a defined employment downturn.
scores.follow_up: What first municipal pilot would you propose, and which cost, service and access measures would determine whether it continues?
scores.confidence: High — all visible response text is readable and the proposals are explicit; personal claims and implementation outcomes are unverified.
scores.narration: Maltby addresses the resident’s main questions with small trials, measured savings, training partnerships and explicit safeguards. Her strongest contribution is a practical decision process. The remaining gap is a concrete financial scenario showing how employment pressure would affect town revenues, costs and services.

scores.strongest_point: Identifies how lost income could reduce local spending and create further business and employment pressures.
scores.biggest_gap: What the Town would do to sustain services and funding if the anticipated employment pressures occur.
scores.follow_up: Which action within Town authority would you support first to protect services and residents if automation reduces local employment?
scores.confidence: Medium — readable text supports the main argument, but “zero based AI or Chat GPU” is ambiguous and key factual examples are unverified.
scores.narration: Carruthers highlights independent judgment and a plausible chain from job losses to weaker retail spending. His aviation example needs further verification. The reply offers little detail about municipal action or public funding, and its economic conclusion exceeds the evidence supplied.

scores.strongest_point: Conditions investment on public value and recognizes the need for continued learning.
scores.biggest_gap: How public services would be financed and workers supported during disruption before any new opportunities materialize.
scores.follow_up: What first investment would you test, and how would you verify net savings while supporting staff whose work changes?
scores.confidence: High — the text is readable and its scope is clear; historical and personal claims remain unverified.
scores.narration: Albano supports continued learning and investment where technology improves public value. His historical analogy offers a reason to consider new opportunities, but does not resolve transition risks. Specific local steps, verified savings and an answer to employment related funding pressure remain undeveloped.

scores.strongest_point: A credible set of municipal use cases is paired with staff expertise, small trials and explicit cost evaluation.
scores.biggest_gap: The candidate’s own technology familiarity and use, followed by the fiscal plan if expected savings do not materialize.
scores.follow_up: Which first staff-led trial would you choose, and what net cost and service thresholds would govern expansion or cancellation?
scores.confidence: High — all visible text is readable and proposals are clearly conditional; feasibility and benefits would still need testing.
scores.narration: Brass proposes concrete municipal uses, staff involvement and small trials with measurable benefits and clear costs. He recognizes household pressure and the limits of technology savings. Personal familiarity, resident safeguards and a fallback budget approach are not demonstrated in this reply.

scores.strongest_point: Connects the discussion to recognizable municipal planning, library and regional traffic applications and a specific learning experience.
scores.biggest_gap: How the Town would maintain funding and support affected residents if efficiencies are insufficient or slow to arrive.
scores.follow_up: What measured result from one of these programs would inform your next budget decision, and what would you do if it shows no net savings?
scores.confidence: Medium — readable text gives specific examples, but several implementation, timing and benefit claims are only partially verified.
scores.narration: Hilson supplies concrete municipal examples and describes relevant learning, while acknowledging uncertainty about future work. Several implementation and savings claims need verification. His funding response depends on efficiencies and wider adaptation, leaving a local transition plan and protections for affected residents unclear.

scores.strongest_point: Keeps essential human expertise and the people delivering services in view, rather than assuming all work is equally replaceable.
scores.biggest_gap: Where funding would come from to sustain the proposed investments if household and business finances weaken.
scores.follow_up: Which training or essential-service investment would you pursue through the Town, with which partners and funding source?
scores.confidence: High — readable text makes its priorities clear; empirical labour claims and implementation remain unverified.
scores.narration: Spurr emphasizes skilled trades, essential workers and preparing young people to use AI. This recognizes valuable human expertise and community needs. The reply does not explain personal technology use, identify a concrete municipal next step or show how continued investment would be financed.

scores.strongest_point: Explicitly considers sharing productivity gains through time rather than assuming displacement is inevitable.
scores.biggest_gap: How shorter hours at unchanged pay would be financed and translated into a municipal funding or service plan.
scores.follow_up: Would you propose a Town or employer-partner trial of shorter hours, and what evidence on net costs and service coverage would justify unchanged pay?
scores.confidence: Medium — the proposal and personal-use statement are readable, but historical causation and productivity assumptions are only partly supported.
scores.narration: Galati proposes sharing productivity gains through shorter hours at unchanged pay, offering an alternative to layoffs. He acknowledges non-use and limits on AI reliance. The proposal still needs evidence of sufficient gains, a municipal role and a plan for funding and service coverage.

scores.strongest_point: A staged municipal adoption process that makes larger spending conditional on measured results and includes residents who cannot comfortably use online services.
scores.biggest_gap: How the Town would maintain services if employment weakens and pilot savings prove too small to offset financial pressure.
scores.follow_up: What would your first municipal technology pilot be, and what net-cost, service-quality and access measures would determine whether it continues?
scores.confidence: High — the visible reply is readable and directly supports the criterion judgments; personal experience and proposed outcomes remain unverified.
scores.narration: Maltby offers a clear municipal approach: test small projects, measure results, protect access and consult expertise. She connects employment pressure to affordability and service demand. The main remaining question is how services would be protected if promised efficiencies do not materialize.

scores.strongest_point: Recognizes that employment losses can affect other businesses through lower consumer spending, rather than considering only directly automated jobs.
scores.biggest_gap: What Halton Hills would actually do to sustain services and public finances under the employment pressure he describes.
scores.follow_up: What specific municipal action would you take first if automation reduced local household spending, and how would it help fund services?
scores.confidence: Medium — the response is readable, but its platform wording is ambiguous and its central aviation examples are only partly checked.
scores.narration: Carruthers highlights worker displacement and the ripple effects of reduced household spending, while valuing independent judgment. His response offers limited municipal action and treats severe economic decline too confidently. Airport examples need further checking, particularly the claimed connection between automation and staffing reductions.

scores.strongest_point: Conditions investment on public value: administrative savings, productivity and service improvement.
scores.biggest_gap: How the Town would fund employees and services if job displacement arrives before new opportunities or municipal savings.
scores.follow_up: What evidence would you require before counting a technology project’s savings in the Town budget, and what would you do if those savings did not arrive?
scores.confidence: High — the text is readable and its coverage and omissions are clear; the historical and personal claims are not independently verified.
scores.narration: Albano supports technology investments that improve services or reduce administrative costs and emphasizes continued learning. His historical analogy offers some perspective on change, but does not resolve transition risks. The reply leaves municipal funding mechanisms, implementation steps and specific safeguards largely undeveloped.

scores.strongest_point: A restrained, testable efficiency proposal grounded in specific municipal operations and staff expertise.
scores.biggest_gap: His own technology familiarity and use are not directly answered; the funding strategy also needs an explicit response if savings fall short.
scores.follow_up: Which of these applications would you test first, and what staff, resident-service and full-cost measures would decide whether to scale it?
scores.confidence: High — readable text clearly supports the restrained reasoning and specific proposals; results of those proposals remain unknown.
scores.narration: Brass proposes practical municipal efficiency trials with staff input, measurable benefits and clear costs. He acknowledges taxpayers’ financial limits and avoids promising technology will solve budget pressures. His own technology use is unanswered, while safeguards and the response to disappointing savings need more detail.

scores.strongest_point: Connects the discussion to concrete municipal and regional applications and describes an effort to learn about planning tools.
scores.biggest_gap: A practical public-funding response if employment changes outpace efficiency gains.
scores.follow_up: For one of the tools you mention, what measured net saving or service improvement would you seek, and how would that affect the Town’s budget during this term?
scores.confidence: Medium — visible text is readable, but several substantive local examples are only partly supported and their benefits are unverified.
scores.narration: Hilson brings concrete local examples and describes learning about municipal technology applications. Several examples have partial support in the shared context, but their claimed efficiencies still need checking. His response recognizes livelihood concerns without explaining how public services would remain funded during disruption.

scores.strongest_point: Keeps the value of human expertise and essential services central to the discussion of technological change.
scores.biggest_gap: How continued investment in public services would be financed if household incomes or business activity weakened.
scores.follow_up: Which training or essential-service initiative could the Town advance first, with which partners, and how would you fund it if revenues or affordability came under pressure?
scores.confidence: High — the response is readable and its priorities and omissions are clear; labour-market claims remain unverified.
scores.narration: Spurr emphasizes skilled trades, human judgment and essential services, offering a people-centered priority for technological change. The reply provides little detail on her own technology use, municipal implementation or funding. Training access and changes within supposedly resilient occupations also deserve attention.

scores.strongest_point: Raises the distribution of productivity gains as a policy choice, including the possibility of protecting wages and improving worker wellbeing.
scores.biggest_gap: What the Town could do to test or advance this idea and how public programmes would remain funded if the assumed productivity gains did not arrive.
scores.follow_up: What evidence and employer or municipal pilot would show that a four-day week can preserve pay, service coverage and financial viability, and what would happen if it cannot?
scores.confidence: Medium — the text is readable, but its key productivity assumption and the precise historical causal story are not established.
scores.narration: Galati proposes sharing productivity gains through shorter hours at unchanged pay and acknowledges limits to AI use. This directly engages worker wellbeing, but assumes large efficiency gains without evidence. The reply needs a feasible municipal role, a funding connection and a fallback if gains disappoint.

scores.biggest_gap: How the Town would fund programs or adapt, and what personal use or familiarity he has.
scores.follow_up: If the Town cannot regulate AI, what would you do locally in the next four years to support affected workers and businesses?
scores.confidence: Medium. The reply is readable but sparse on mechanisms.

responses.transcript:
Thank you for raising this. Technology deserves more attention in this election because it touches jobs, local businesses, municipal services and how we spend taxpayers' money.

As a business owner and founder of Earth Credit Canada, technology is part of my work. I'm comfortable using digital tools and exploring new applications, while recognizing that AI, quantum computing, robotics and 3D printing each require different expertise. A councillor must be willing to learn, ask informed questions and seek qualified advice.

I see AI as a tool in a toolbox, something to help us, not something to become completely reliant on. When we ask AI to write a script, it needs prompts, inputs and direction. We still have a responsibility to check its work, apply our judgment and stand behind the results.

As your Ward 1 councillor, I would advocate for a practical technology plan with regular reviews. We should identify where technology could improve services, test it through small projects and measure the results before committing significant money. Faster applications, easier access to information and less repetitive administration are areas worth exploring. Privacy, cybersecurity, human oversight and access for residents who aren't comfortable online must be part of that work.

I also want us to work with businesses, schools and training providers to help residents develop new skills and attract employers to Acton. Our youth should have opportunities to learn about these technologies and build careers here.

Your funding question is a serious one. If people lose employment or income, their ability to pay taxes suffers, while demand for public support may grow. We cannot assume that taxpayers can simply absorb increasing costs.

My approach would be to scrutinize spending, use technology where it delivers measurable savings, support a diverse local economy and plan for different financial scenarios. Savings should help protect essential services and keep taxes manageable. Where responsibilities extend beyond the Town, we need to advocate with regional, provincial and federal partners.

Technology is moving forward, and we cannot afford to be left behind. We need to prepare thoughtfully, bring our community along and make sure progress benefits the people who live here.

Thanks for the question Chris. Since the beginning of my campaign, I have been mentioning candidates in an election should not be using AI to answer questions. We first need councillors to have their own thoughts on the future of AI. The reliance of AI today is alarming. My platform is zero based AI or Chat GPU.

My concern about the future of AI and the impact it will have on the workforce in the future. Having just retired from the aviation community, it is again alarming to see how many airlines are pushing for the advancement of AI tools to lesson the work force. At some airports in Eastern Asia are already using AI tools were a passenger does not have to interact with any airline employee through the whole checkin. This facial recognition AI is also started entering airports in America.

There will be some absolute possibilities with AI as well. It could really help the medical fields and potentially cure some diseases. The municipalities do not have much say in regulating AI but all levels of government should be looking at the burden it could put on our unemployment rates. This puts stress on all the citizens and businesses. Limited spending is needed when unemployed which means retailers suffer and they lay of staff. It's just a slippery slope to the ruining of our economy.

Thank you for the questions, Chris.

I have been using technology in one form or another throughout my working career and during my time on Council. In fact, I'm using technology right now to respond to this post.

We can't avoid technology it is everywhere, and it is changing by the minute. For me, being familiar with technology means continuing to learn.

AI and other technologies are going to change the way we work. I believe that we need to adopt the changes while using them responsibly and where they provide real value. We should invest in technology when it can reduce administrative costs, improve productivity and improve services.

We have seen this before. During the Industrial Revolution, there were many concerns that new technologies would replace workers and eliminate jobs. While technology did change the workforce, it also created new opportunities and changed the way we lived and worked.

In my opinion, we need to keep up with changes and don't fear them.

Chris, thanks for raising this.

As Mayor, I would focus on finding efficiencies that may not be visible today. Could better technology identify duplicate work, reduce paperwork, uncover purchasing savings, improve scheduling or flag maintenance issues before they become expensive repairs? Those are opportunities worth exploring with the staff who understand our services best.

The goal is to give our employees better tools and more time to serve residents.

AI, robotics, 3D printing and quantum computing have different potential uses. We should stay informed, work with knowledgeable partners and test practical applications on a small scale, with measurable benefits and clear costs.

Your question about funding is important too. If employment and household incomes come under pressure, we cannot simply assume taxpayers can absorb ever-increasing costs. We need to scrutinize spending, uncover savings and strengthen our local economy by attracting businesses that provide good careers.

Technology alone will not solve our budget challenges. Still, we should explore how it can help us make better decisions, stretch tax dollars further and maintain the services residents depend on.

Thanks for the question, Chris, and apologies for the slow response. The speed of technology is continuing to increase and I think it's tough for many sectors, including government, to keep track. I do use technology and am as familiar with it as I think most adults are in this day and age.

At the Ontario Municipal Conference a year or two back, I attended a session on using AI and computer modelling to better plan municipal budgeting, repairs and forecasting. The Province put forth legislation a couple years ago about Asset Management which is making municipalities categorize and record all their infrastructure so we can better plan and budget going forward. Halton Hills has gone through this process and I support it. The Town has also continued to roll out Copilot licenses to help make staff more efficient. Meanwhile, our library (where I have served on their board) is using 3D printing to print medals for Battle of the Books and for other activities, saving us time and making us more efficient. At the Regional level, the Region is starting to use technology to make smarter intersections where traffic lights better respond to actual traffic volumes at different times of day rather than using the same time intervals whether there is traffic or not. There are, of course, all sorts of examples and the possibilities are nearly endless. We will need to continue to monitor what those possibilities are and I support being creative with what those possibilities might be.

To your question about funding the public sector as the private sector sheds jobs, I think we are really only at the start of the next technological revolution. In my mind, it's very tough to imagine how different our working lives and different sectors might look in the next couple decades as automation continues to a whole new level. We need to use the tools available to us and benefit from those efficiencies. People will still need jobs or ways of feeding their families, though, and I think we will navigate those changes with the rest of society as things continue to change (as we have in the past with other major technological revolutions throughout history).

Hi Chris,

There's no doubt that AI is advancing at record speed, and we need to stay informed and adaptable as these technologies evolve.

When it comes to the public and private sectors, I think we've already seen a major shift from when our generation entered post-secondary education to where we are today. We were often encouraged to believe university was the primary path to success, whereas today, we're doing a much better job of showing young people the opportunities and earning potential that come with skilled trades. I see this first hand every day. We still have a shortage of skilled trade workers but I'm hopeful the numbers will continue to climb.

COVID also gave us a clear picture of how important essential workers are to keeping our communities running. As society changes, our priorities need to evolve with it. We must continue investing in firefighters, police officers, paramedics, healthcare workers and skilled tradespeople whose hands-on expertise and human judgment are difficult to replace with AI.

The next generation entering the workforce will have grown up with AI much like our generation grew up with social media. We need to prepare them to use these tools effectively while ensuring we continue to value the people, skills and essential services our communities depend on and we as leaders need to be prepared as well.

I'm not a user of AI, perhaps to my detriment as I know that it can be a useful tool if applied correctly. I know that it can help us be more efficient and cut down on a lot of tasks like proofreading, editing and sourcing of references. However, it shouldn't be used exclusively for writing reports or other relevant documents required in the workplace.

As far as employers laying off workers, I believe that instead they could cut their hours back substantially while still paying them their regular wages. The super efficiency of AI would still allow them to turn a profit while giving their staff a much needed break. I reference a time when Mr Ford from the Ford Motor Company started using automation to build his vehicles, relying less on hands on performance from his staff. Well what did he do? Instead of laying off workers, he gave them Saturdays off! At the time, most people were working 6 day weeks. He was one of the first to go to a 5 day work week. Maybe we need to take that a step further and start giving workers a 4 day work week since the use of AI is improving efficiency by a large margin. It's been talked about before and I believe it's a relevant conversation to have again.

scenes.title: Plan for more than one future.
scenes.narration: The advice is to prepare for more than one pace of change. For gradual adoption, measure real gains and build skills. For rapid disruption, track local pressure and coordinate a response with the governments responsible. If promised savings disappoint, protect priority services and use a funded fallback. These are planning scenarios, not forecasts or claims that job losses are inevitable.
